title: Ottawa begins rolling out $700-million in AI compute funding under new sector-based approach
html:
AI Minister Evan Solomon speaks during the All-In conference in Montreal in September. On Thursday, he shared details of Ottawa’s plans to distribute $700-million in previously announced funding.Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press

The federal government is opening up $700-million in funding to help Canadian companies pay for the processing power they need to develop artificial intelligence applications, while trying to steer them to homegrown providers of that increasingly scarce resource.

The AI boom has generated massive demand for compute – the technology sector’s term for processing power – and driven a multitrillion-dollar build out of data centres and other digital infrastructure around the world. But Silicon Valley giants and lavishly funded startups have already bought up much of the existing and new capacity. As a result, smaller companies outside the tech sector often struggle to find and afford the processing power to offer their own AI products and services.

Ottawa’s AI Compute Access Fund – first launched in March 2025 with a $300-million budget – is meant to address that challenge. The program provides subsidies or financing to companies that spend between $100,000 and $5-million on processing power for technology R&D projects. Early rounds were heavily oversubscribed. The federal government increased the fund’s budget to $1-billion as part of the national AI strategy launched in June.

AI Minister Evan Solomon on Thursday announced Ottawa’s plans to distribute the additional $700-million. Canadian small- and medium-sized firms “need the fuel to get going, and it’s expensive, and it’s a constraint,” he said in an interview prior to the announcement. “We wanted to address that.”

On Thursday, Mr. Solomon also announced more funding under the program’s first phase, with 45 companies set to get more than $52-million between them.

Companies have previously complained that the program had been slow to choose recipients and to distribute the money to them. In response, Mr. Solomon said Ottawa is modifying the program going forward to accept applications on an industry basis, starting with companies in health and life sciences. Ottawa plans to launch all those funding calls by the end of 2027. Other priority sectors identified in the national AI strategy include agriculture, transportation, energy and natural resources, and manufacturing and robotics.

Mr. Solomon said the fund will also use AI tools made by Toronto-based Cohere to conduct analysis and risk assessments of applications, although human officials will still make final decisions. And the program is being expanded to fund non-profits and postsecondary institutes.

One of the recipients announced Wednesday, Apera AI, has faced more difficulty to buy access to the most advanced AI infrastructure this year, according to chief executive Sina Afrooze. The Vancouver-based company’s technology makes the robots in its clients’ factories more reliable and productive.

Apera is competing for limited available capacity against frontier AI developers such as Anthropic PBC ANT-Q and OpenAI, which spend a lot more. “What that translates into for us is slower pace of R&D,” said Mr. Afrooze, adding that training a model might now take two weeks instead of one. “The iteration is slower, and our engineers are far less productive.”

Compute is Apera’s single largest expense. The company spends up to US$4-million a year on processing power to train or tweak its AI models. The federal funding – Apera is set to receive up to $921,600 – should help offset some of those costs, Mr. Afrooze said.

The cloud services arms of U.S. tech giants remain the main sellers of compute to Canadian companies. Apera currently buys from both Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud.

Ottawa is also trying to encourage the growth of domestic alternatives, as it seeks to foster Canada’s AI ecosystem and secure its economic and geopolitical sovereignty. The fund already offers a bigger subsidy to companies if they buy processing power that’s generated within the country. But it plans to boost the payback share to four-fifths of recipients’ compute costs if they use providers that are Canadian-incorporated, -controlled and -owned.

“That’s going to incentivize not just people who want to take [compute], but people who want to provide it,” Mr. Solomon said.

Canadian cloud providers who compete with the U.S. giants include Denvr Dataworks Corp., Micrologic and ThinkOn Inc.

Toronto-based Gotcare (legally A2B Directcare Inc.) currently also uses Amazon Web Services. But the company is looking to switch its compute purchases over to domestic suppliers with up to $604,747 from the federal compute program.

Gotcare connects home health workers to patients that need on-call care, using AI to match them based on proximity, medical condition, the language spoken and other factors. Its systems can also predict when a client might need a visit.

The federal funding will let Gotcare buy more capacity to train and test its own clinical AI models, and develop its software, said CEO Chenny Xia. And switching to domestic cloud services could reduce the cost of regulatory compliance, which she said deters Canadian health technology companies from using AI.

Other companies receiving funding in the government’s latest round include regulatory software startup Ultimarii Ltd., visual effects studio Monsters Aliens Robots Zombies Inc., drug discovery company Congruence Therapeutics Inc. and vertical agriculture innovator NuLeaf Farms.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article stated that the AI Compute Access Fund was providing 45 companies with more than $55 million, based on information provided ahead of publication by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada. The fund will be providing over $52 million to those companies.
summary: Forty-five companies to get $52-million in cloud subsidies as government seeks to speed up funding decisions
